subject: Mathematics

unit.unitOverview: Welcome to Unit 9! In this unit you become a data detective. Statistics is the part of mathematics that helps us collect information, record it neatly, show it in pictures, and then read those pictures to answer questions about the world. Every day people ask questions like ‘Which fruit do most children like?’ or ‘How many goats came to the well today?’ Statistics gives you the tools to answer questions like these carefully and fairly.
learningPath: Preview the goals and core ideas
Learn methods and study worked examples
Complete guided practice, activities and games
Apply, explain and complete the Unit Challenge

provenance.transformation: Structured from the Cambridge Primary Mathematics 0096 — Stage 2 workbook source documents for screen presentation.

outcomes: Ask a good survey question and collect data fairly from a group of people.
Record data quickly and neatly using tally marks and a frequency table.
Sort objects and numbers into groups using lists, tables and Venn diagrams.
Read a pictogram where one symbol stands for more than one item.
Make your own pictogram with a clear key.
Read and build a block graph (bar graph) with a title and labels.
Interpret data to answer questions: most, least, total, and how many more.
Choose the best way to show a set of data and explain your choice.

concepts.title: Collecting Data with a Good Question
concepts.explanation:
Before you can draw any chart, you first need some data to draw. Data is simply information you gather. The most common way to gather data is a survey – you ask a group of people the same question and write down every answer. The very first step is to choose a clear question with a small set of answers to choose from.

Imagine Amina wants to find out the favourite fruit of the children at Nuur Academy. A good question is: ‘Which of these fruits do you like best: mango, banana, papaya or dates?’ This is a good question because it is clear and it gives everyone the same choices. A poor question would be ‘Do you like nice fruit?’ because ‘nice’ means different things to different people, and there are no clear choices to count.

A good survey question is also fair. A fair question does not push people towards one answer. If Farah asked ‘You love football, don’t you?’ she is pushing people to say yes – that is not fair, and the data would be spoiled. Instead she should ask ‘Which sport do you like best: football, running, swimming or wrestling?’ Now every sport has an equal chance, and the data will be honest.
concepts.example: You must also decide who to ask and how many people. If you only ask your two best friends, you do not learn much about the whole class. The more people you ask – within reason – the more you can trust your answer. When Hassan surveyed all 20 children in his group instead of just a few, his results told a much more complete story. Asking a good number of people fairly is the secret to trustworthy data.

concepts.title: Recording Data with Tally Charts
concepts.explanation:
When you ask people a question, the answers come quickly, one after another. You need a fast way to keep count without losing track. The best tool for this is the tally mark. A tally mark is a single straight line, and each line stands for one. You draw one line for every answer you hear.

Tally marks have a clever trick for counting in fives. You draw four straight lines, and then the fifth line goes across the other four, like a little gate. This makes a bundle of five that is very easy to count. So |||| (four lines) means four, and a crossed gate means five. Two gates and three more lines would be 5 + 5 + 3 = 13. Counting in fives is much faster than counting single lines one by one.

Let us record a real example. Khadija asks ten friends which drink they like best – camel milk, water, or juice – and hears these answers in order: camel milk, water, camel milk, juice, camel milk, water, camel milk, juice, water, camel milk. As each answer comes, she adds one tally mark next to that drink. At the end she counts the marks in each row. This is called making a tally chart.

Once all the marks are drawn, you turn them into numbers. The number of marks in each row is called the frequency – it tells you how often that answer came up. When you write each group next to its frequency in a neat table, you have made a frequency table. Here is Khadija's finished frequency table:
concepts.example: Notice that the three frequencies add up to 5 + 3 + 2 = 10, which is exactly how many friends Khadija asked. This is a wonderful way to check your work: the totals in a frequency table should always add up to the number of people or things you counted. If they do not match, a tally mark has been missed or counted twice, and you should count again. Being careful and checking is the mark of a true data detective.

concepts.title: Sorting Data with Lists, Tables and Venn Diagrams
concepts.explanation:
Data is much easier to understand when it is sorted into groups. There are several neat ways to sort. The simplest is a list. You can put a list in a sensible order – smallest to largest, or in alphabetical order. If Omar has the heights 125 cm, 118 cm and 129 cm, he can order them from shortest to tallest: 118 cm, 125 cm, 129 cm. A well-ordered list makes it easy to spot the smallest and the largest at a glance.

A table sorts data into rows and columns, and it can hold more than one fact about each item. A table has a heading at the top of every column so you know what each column means. For example, a table about children might have columns for name, favourite colour and number of pets. To read a table, you find the right row and slide across to the right column. Tables are powerful because they organise several facts at once, all lined up neatly.

A Venn diagram is a special sorting tool made of circles. Each circle stands for one group. The clever part is that the circles overlap in the middle. An item that belongs to both groups goes in the overlap, which we call the intersection. An item that belongs to neither group goes outside both circles. This lets us show items that fit in more than one group at the same time.
concepts.example: Let us sort some animals with Idris. His two groups are ‘Lives in water’ and ‘Has fur’. A fish lives in water but has no fur, so it goes in the water circle only. A cat has fur but does not live in water, so it goes in the fur circle only. A seal both lives in water and has fur, so it goes in the overlap in the middle. A bird does neither, so it sits outside both circles. Reading a Venn diagram means looking carefully at each region and saying which items you find there.

concepts.title: Pictograms – Showing Data with Pictures
concepts.explanation:
A pictogram is a chart that uses small pictures or symbols to show how many. Pictograms are friendly and colourful, and they make it very easy to see which group is the biggest just by looking. In a pictogram, each group has its own row, and you draw a symbol for the amounts. The longer the row of symbols, the more there are.

The most important part of a pictogram is the key. The key tells you what one symbol is worth. Sometimes one symbol stands for just one item, but often one symbol stands for several items, to save drawing hundreds of pictures. For example, if the key says each 🍦 stands for 5 ice creams, then a row with 3 ice-cream symbols means 3 × 5 = 15 ice creams. Always read the key first, before you count anything.

Let us read a pictogram with Zahra. It shows ice creams sold at a shop over three days, and the key says each 🍦 = 5 ice creams. Monday has 3 symbols, Tuesday has 5 symbols, and Wednesday has 2 symbols. To find each day's sales, multiply the symbols by 5: Monday = 3 × 5 = 15, Tuesday = 5 × 5 = 25, Wednesday = 2 × 5 = 10. To find which day was busiest, look for the longest row: Tuesday, with the most symbols, sold the most ice creams.

Pictograms are also good for finding how many more. To see how many more ice creams were sold on Tuesday than on Wednesday, first find each total: Tuesday is 25 and Wednesday is 10. Then subtract: 25 − 10 = 15 more ice creams. And to find the total for all three days, add them: 15 + 25 + 10 = 50 ice creams. Reading, multiplying, subtracting and adding all come together in one friendly chart.
concepts.example: When you make your own pictogram, you have three jobs. First, choose a symbol that suits your topic – a little goat for counting goats, a drop for water. Second, decide what each symbol is worth and write it in the key; if your numbers are large, let one symbol stand for 2, 5 or 10. Third, draw the symbols neatly in rows, all the same size, so the rows can be compared fairly. Sometimes you will need half a symbol to show half of the key value – if one symbol is 10 books, then half a symbol shows 5 books.

concepts.title: Block Graphs – Building Bars of Data
concepts.explanation:
A block graph, also called a bar graph, shows data using blocks stacked into bars. Each group has its own bar, and the taller the bar, the more there are. Block graphs are excellent for comparing amounts at a glance, because your eyes can quickly see which bar is tallest and which is shortest.

Every good block graph has some important parts. It has a title at the top that says what the graph is about, like ‘Favourite Colours’. It has labels along the bottom telling you what each bar stands for, such as red, blue, green and yellow. And it has numbers up the side, called the scale, telling you how much each block is worth. To read a bar, you look at the top of the bar and read across to the number on the scale.

Let us read a block graph with Maryam. It shows favourite colours in her class. The red bar reaches 4, the blue bar reaches 10, the green bar reaches 8 and the yellow bar reaches 8. To answer ‘Which colour is most popular?’ she looks for the tallest bar – blue, at 10. To answer ‘How many chose red?’ she reads the top of the red bar – 4. To find ‘How many more chose blue than red?’ she subtracts: 10 − 4 = 6 more. And the total surveyed is 4 + 10 + 8 + 8 = 30 children.

Sometimes the scale does not go up in ones. On a busy graph, each step might be worth 2, or 5, or 10. This is the graph's scale, and you must read it carefully. If each block is worth 2 goats and a bar is 5 blocks tall, then that bar stands for 5 × 2 = 10 goats, not 5. Reading the scale wrongly is a common slip, so always check what one block is worth before you say a total.
concepts.example: When you build your own block graph, work in careful steps. Write a clear title. Draw a line up the side for the scale and mark the numbers evenly. Draw a bar for each group, making its height match the amount using the scale. Keep every bar the same width and leave small equal gaps between them, so the comparison is fair. Finally, label each bar underneath. A neat block graph tells its story instantly, with no words needed.

concepts.title: Interpreting Data – Reading the Story
concepts.explanation:
Making a chart is only half the work. The real prize is interpreting it – reading the chart to answer questions and tell the story hidden in the numbers. Good data detectives ask the same few questions of every chart, whether it is a tally chart, a pictogram or a block graph.

The first question is ‘Which group has the most?’ In a tally chart or table, this is the row with the biggest frequency. In a pictogram it is the longest row of symbols. In a block graph it is the tallest bar. The second question is the opposite: ‘Which group has the least?’ – the smallest frequency, the shortest row, or the shortest bar.

The third question is ‘How many altogether?’ To answer this you add every group's amount together. The fourth question is ‘How many more does one group have than another?’ To answer this you subtract the smaller amount from the larger. These four questions – most, least, total, and difference – unlock almost any chart you will ever meet. When Abdi practised asking these four questions on every graph, reading data became easy and even fun.

There is one more skill: describing what you notice in words. A good data detective does not only give numbers; they explain the story. Maryam might say, ‘Blue was the most popular colour, and twice as many children chose blue as chose red.’ Using clear comparing words such as more than, less than, most, least and the same as helps you explain your findings so that anyone can understand them.

You have now met six big ideas: collecting data with a fair question, recording it with tally charts and frequency tables, sorting it with lists, tables and Venn diagrams, showing it with pictograms, showing it with block graphs, and interpreting the story the data tells. These ideas are not separate islands – they work together in one journey from question to answer.

Think of a full data adventure. First Amina asks a fair question at Nuur Academy: ‘Which fruit do you like best?’ Then she records every answer with tally marks and makes a frequency table. Next she chooses a way to show the data – perhaps a pictogram with a mango symbol, or a block graph with coloured bars. Finally she interprets her chart, telling the class that mango was the favourite and that three more children chose mango than chose dates. Question, record, show, interpret – that is the whole cycle of statistics.
concepts.example: The best way to lock these ideas into your memory is to run the whole cycle yourself with real things at home. Ask your family a fun question, tally their answers, build a little chart, and read out what you found. Every time you do this, you become a stronger data detective, and the harder graphs you meet in later years will feel friendly and familiar. Now let us practise together with some worked examples.

methods.title: How to make a tally chart
methods.example: A tally chart shows mango as a gate of five and three more single marks. How many chose mango?
steps: Write each group in its own row.
Make one tally mark for every answer you hear.
Make every fifth mark a gate across the other four.
Count the marks to find each frequency, then check they add to your total.

methods.title: How to read a pictogram
methods.example: In a survey of 12 children, 5 chose banana and 4 chose papaya. The rest chose dates. How many chose dates?
steps: Read the key to see what one symbol is worth.
Count the symbols in the row.
Multiply the number of symbols by the key value.
For half a symbol, add half of the key value.

methods.title: How to read a block graph
methods.example: Sort these into ‘Even numbers’ and ‘Greater than 10’: 6, 9, 12, 18, 21. Which numbers go in the overlap?
steps: Read the title to see what the graph is about.
Read the scale up the side to see what each block is worth.
Find the top of the bar and read across to the scale.
Compare bars: the tallest is the most, the shortest is the least.

methods.title: Reading a pictogram
methods.example: A pictogram of books read has a key of 📚 = 10 books. Class B shows 6 symbols. How many books did Class B read?
steps: Each symbol is worth 10, and there are 6 symbols.
So 6 × 10 = 60 books.
Reading the key first told us each picture was worth 10, not 1.

methods.title: How many more in a pictogram
methods.example: Using the same key of 10, Class A shows 4 symbols and Class B shows 6 symbols. How many more books did Class B read?
steps: Class A = 4 × 10 = 40 books.
Class B = 6 × 10 = 60 books.
The difference is 60 − 40 = 20 more books for Class B.

methods.title: Reading a block graph
methods.example: A block graph shows goals scored: Lions 8, Tigers 12, Bears 6, Eagles 10. Which team scored the most, and how many did all teams score together?
steps: The tallest bar is the Tigers at 12 goals, so they scored the most.
For the total, add every bar: 8 + 12 + 6 + 10 = 36 goals altogether.
Check your total by adding the four bars again in a different order.

workedExamples.title: Reading tally marks
workedExamples.prompt: A tally chart shows mango as a gate of five and three more single marks. How many chose mango?
workedExamples.solution: A gate is 5, and three single marks add 3 more. So 5 + 3 = 8 children chose mango. The gate lets us count in fives, which is quicker than counting eight single lines.

workedExamples.title: Completing a frequency table
workedExamples.prompt: In a survey of 12 children, 5 chose banana and 4 chose papaya. The rest chose dates. How many chose dates?
workedExamples.solution: So far 5 + 4 = 9 children are counted. The survey had 12 children in all, so the dates group must be 12 − 9 = 3 children. Always use the total to check the parts add up correctly.

workedExamples.title: Sorting in a Venn diagram
workedExamples.prompt: Sort these into ‘Even numbers’ and ‘Greater than 10’: 6, 9, 12, 18, 21. Which numbers go in the overlap?
workedExamples.solution: The overlap holds numbers that are both even and greater than 10. Check each: 12 is even and greater than 10 — yes. 18 is even and greater than 10 — yes. So 12 and 18 go in the overlap. (6 is even but not greater than 10; 21 is greater than 10 but not even; 9 is neither.)

workedExamples.title: Reading a pictogram
workedExamples.prompt: A pictogram of books read has a key of 📚 = 10 books. Class B shows 6 symbols. How many books did Class B read?
workedExamples.solution: Each symbol is worth 10, and there are 6 symbols. So 6 × 10 = 60 books. Reading the key first told us each picture was worth 10, not 1.

workedExamples.title: How many more in a pictogram
workedExamples.prompt: Using the same key of 10, Class A shows 4 symbols and Class B shows 6 symbols. How many more books did Class B read?
workedExamples.solution: Class A = 4 × 10 = 40 books. Class B = 6 × 10 = 60 books. The difference is 60 − 40 = 20 more books for Class B.

workedExamples.title: Reading a block graph
workedExamples.prompt: A block graph shows goals scored: Lions 8, Tigers 12, Bears 6, Eagles 10. Which team scored the most, and how many did all teams score together?
workedExamples.solution: The tallest bar is the Tigers at 12 goals, so they scored the most. For the total, add every bar: 8 + 12 + 6 + 10 = 36 goals altogether.

workedExamples.title: Reading a scale that jumps in twos
workedExamples.prompt: On a block graph each block is worth 2 goats. Farah's bar is 5 blocks tall. How many goats does her bar show?
workedExamples.solution: Each block is worth 2, and the bar is 5 blocks tall, so 5 × 2 = 10 goats. If we had forgotten the scale and said 5, we would have been badly wrong. Always read the scale first.

workedExamples.title: Choosing the best chart
workedExamples.prompt: Hassan wants to show which children play football AND also have a pet. Which sorting tool should he use, and why?
workedExamples.solution: He should use a Venn diagram, because it has an overlap that shows items belonging to both groups at once. A list or a single bar could not show the ‘both’ group clearly, but the intersection of a Venn diagram is made exactly for this.

workedExamples.title: How many children were surveyed in total
workedExamples.prompt: How many children were surveyed in total?
workedExamples.solution: Add every frequency together: 5 + 7 + 3 + 2 = 17. So 17 children were surveyed in total.

workedExamples.title: Practice 10
workedExamples.prompt: How many more children chose dog than chose rabbit?
workedExamples.solution: Dog was chosen by 7 children and rabbit by 3 children. 7 − 3 = 4, so 4 more children chose dog than rabbit.

workedExamples.title: Practice 11
workedExamples.prompt: A pictogram key says each 📚 = 10 books. Class A has 4 symbols, Class B has 6 symbols, Class C has 3 symbols. How many books did each class read?
workedExamples.solution: Each symbol is worth 10 books. Class A: 4 × 10 = 40 books. Class B: 6 × 10 = 60 books. Class C: 3 × 10 = 30 books.

workedExamples.title: Practice 12
workedExamples.prompt: Using the same pictogram, how many books were read by all three classes together?
workedExamples.solution: Add each class's total: 40 + 60 + 30 = 130 books read altogether.

activities.title: Family Favourites Survey
steps: Choose a fair question with four choices, such as ‘Which fruit do you like best: mango, banana, papaya or dates?’
Ask everyone in your family and use tally marks to record each answer.
Turn your tallies into a frequency table with a number for each fruit.
Add up all the frequencies and check the total matches how many people you asked.
Keep your frequency table – you will use it to build a chart in Activity 3.

activities.title: Tally Marks Counting Game
activities.materials: a window or doorway where you can watch things go past.
steps: Choose three things to count, such as cars, goats and people.
Watch for ten minutes and make a tally mark each time you see one.
Remember to make every fifth mark a gate across the other four.
Count your gates in fives, then add the extra marks. Which did you see most of?

activities.title: Build a Pictogram
activities.materials: the frequency table from Activity 1, paper and colours.
steps: Choose a simple symbol for your topic, such as a small circle or a fruit shape.
Decide what each symbol is worth and write it in a key (for small numbers, one symbol = one).
Draw a row of symbols for each fruit, all the same size, matching your frequencies.
Show your pictogram to your family and ask them which fruit was the favourite.

activities.title: Block Graph with Household Objects
activities.materials: small objects such as bottle caps, stones or dry beans, and a flat table.
steps: Pick three or four groups to compare, such as spoons, cups and plates in your kitchen.
Count how many of each and lay the objects in straight columns, one object per block.
Line the columns up side by side so they look like the bars of a block graph.
Look along the tops of the columns: which is tallest (most) and which is shortest (least)?

activities.title: Venn Diagram Sorting Investigation
activities.materials: two loops of string or two drawn circles that overlap, and a pile of objects.
steps: Label one circle ‘Round’ and the other circle ‘Can roll’.
Take objects from around the house and decide where each one goes.
Put objects that are both round and can roll in the overlap in the middle.
Count how many objects are round altogether, remembering to include the overlap.

activities.title: Data Detective Family Game
activities.materials: your family or friends and the four detective questions.
steps: Show your family the pictogram or block graph you made earlier.
Take turns asking the four detective questions: most, least, total, and how many more.
Give a point for each correct answer and see who becomes the top data detective.
Then let a family member ask you a tricky question about the chart.

After your activities, talk or write about: Which activity helped you understand data best? Was it easier to read a pictogram or a block graph? What survey would you like to carry out next? Share your answer with your teacher at your next session.

rules.title: Tally Mark Rule
rules.text: One straight line means one. Every fifth mark goes across the group of four to make a gate of five. Count the gates in fives first, then add the extra single marks.

rules.title: Pictogram Key Rule
rules.text: Always read the key first. One symbol may be worth more than one item. Symbols times key value = the total. Half a symbol shows half the key value.

rules.title: Block Graph Scale Rule
rules.text: Read the scale up the side first. One block does not always mean one. The tallest bar shows the most; the shortest bar shows the least.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: A pictogram key says each 🐐 = 10 goats. A row shows 4 and a half symbols. How many goats is that? Explain the half symbol.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: 1) 4 × 10 = 40, plus half a symbol = 5, so 45 goats; the half symbol is half of the key value (half of 10 is 5).

reasoningPrompts.prompt: On a block graph each block is worth 2 children. The football bar is 7 blocks tall. How many children chose football?
A block graph shows rainfall where each block is worth 5 cm: January 2 blocks, February 3 blocks, March 4 blocks. How much rain fell in total?
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: Add the blocks: 2 + 3 + 4 = 9 blocks. Each block is worth 5 cm, so 9 × 5 = 45 cm of rain fell in total.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Waris says a pictogram is always better than a block graph. Is this always, sometimes, or never true? Explain with an example.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: Sometimes true. A pictogram is good for showing simple counts with pictures, but a block graph is better for showing larger or more precise numbers, since drawing many symbols can be harder to read than a tall bar. Neither is always better — it depends on the data.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Explain the key idea in Block Graphs – Building Bars of Data.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer:
A block graph, also called a bar graph, shows data using blocks stacked into bars. Each group has its own bar, and the taller the bar, the more there are. Block graphs are excellent for comparing amounts at a glance, because your eyes can quickly see which bar is tallest and which is shortest.

Every good block graph has some important parts. It has a title at the top that says what the graph is about, like ‘Favourite Colours’. It has labels along the bottom telling you what each bar stands for, such as red, blue, green and yellow. And it has numbers up the side, called the scale, telling you how much each block is worth. To read a bar, you look at the top of the bar and read across to the number on the scale.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Explain the key idea in Interpreting Data – Reading the Story.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer:
Making a chart is only half the work. The real prize is interpreting it – reading the chart to answer questions and tell the story hidden in the numbers. Good data detectives ask the same few questions of every chart, whether it is a tally chart, a pictogram or a block graph.

The first question is ‘Which group has the most?’ In a tally chart or table, this is the row with the biggest frequency. In a pictogram it is the longest row of symbols. In a block graph it is the tallest bar. The second question is the opposite: ‘Which group has the least?’ – the smallest frequency, the shortest row, or the shortest bar.

selfAssessment: I can ask a good survey question and collect data fairly from a group of people.
I can record data quickly and neatly using tally marks and a frequency table.
I can sort objects and numbers into groups using lists, tables and Venn diagrams.
I can read a pictogram where one symbol stands for more than one item.
I can make your own pictogram with a clear key.
I can read and build a block graph (bar graph) with a title and labels.
I can interpret data to answer questions: most, least, total, and how many more.
I can choose the best way to show a set of data and explain your choice.
